Multi-Environment GWAS with wgAim

Author

Julian Taylor & Ari Verbyla

Published

August 3, 2026

1 Overview

This vignette demonstrates the multi-environment extension of the wgAim GWAS pipeline for a diversity panel evaluated across several field trials. The framework detects markers whose effects are consistent across trials (main-effect QTL, MAIN) as well as markers whose effects differ between trials (G×E interaction QTL, INT), within a unified forward-selection model — exactly as the multivariate qtlAim() engine does for biparental crosses.

The pipeline has the same three stages as the univariate GWAS analysis:

  1. Pre-analysis — check, filter and prime the diversity panel with checkPanel(), filterPanel() and primePanel().
  2. Analysis — develop a multi-trial base model and run gwasAim() with the Trait argument set to the grouping factor (here "Site").
  3. Post-analysis — interrogate, summarise, and visualise the detected markers using summary(), plot(), and aimTrace().

The Trait argument is a general grouping factor: it may represent sites, trials, environments, seasons, or measured traits — any factor whose levels define the multivariate response. In this vignette Trait = "Site".

Throughout we use the genoGWASraw, mapGWASsim and phenoGWASsim datasets bundled with the package: a simulated diversity panel of 200 lines genotyped at approximately 1700 SNP markers across 10 chromosomes (~170 markers per chromosome, average spacing ~0.9 cM), evaluated in 6 field sites with 2 replicates each. The panel is generated with AlphaSimR — 50 founder haplotypes via a coalescent (runMacs2), one generation of random mating to produce 200 F1 diverse lines, then a SNP chip actively selected from segregating sites with minor allele frequency (MAF) > 0.15. All shipped markers have F1 MAF > 0.15 (median ~0.32), giving a kinship matrix \boldsymbol{K} with genuine full-rank structure (off-diagonal SD ~0.085) that captures the half-sib / full-sib relatedness naturally. Yields are on the tonnes-per-hectare scale (site means 4.5–4.9 t/ha, residual SD ~0.377 t/ha per site) with two Kronecker-structured polygenic components matching the multivariate analysis’s fa(Site,k):vm(id, K) + fa(Site,k):id decomposition (both kept deliberately small so the composite LRT stops cleanly once true QTL are absorbed). Five QTL were planted at known positions to give ground truth for detection: three with consistent effects across all sites (Chr2 +0.145 t/ha, Chr5 −0.145 t/ha, Chr7 +0.125 t/ha — the third is the weakest MAIN) and two with site-specific effects (Chr3 fading from +0.230 t/ha in Env1 to 0 in Env6; Chr9 crossing from −0.180 t/ha in Env1–Env3 to +0.180 t/ha in Env4–Env6). The raw marker matrix contains realistic data-quality issues (missingness, monomorphic markers, duplicate lines, duplicate markers, unplaceable markers) so the full pre-analysis pipeline can be exercised. See the roxygen help for ?phenoGWASsim for the full specification.

Requires: ASReml-R V4. The vignette is pre-rendered so no licence is needed to read it. Run the code chunks only if you have ASReml-R installed.

2 Mathematical Framework

The mathematical framework underpinning multi-environment gwasAim() is essentially identical to that of multivariate qtlAim(). Please see the Mathematical Framework section of the Multivariate QTL Mapping vignette for the full development, covering:

  • the stacked multivariate LMM \boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\tau} + \boldsymbol{Z}_u\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{g} + \boldsymbol{e} with block-diagonal residual and cross-trial genetic covariance matrix \boldsymbol{G}_a;
  • factor analytic (FA) parsimonious approximation \boldsymbol{G}_a = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\top} + \boldsymbol{\Psi} that keeps the parameter count manageable for many trials;
  • decomposition of the genetic term into a composite additive component \boldsymbol{a} (via the vm/mbf paths — vm typically used for diversity panels) and a residual polygenic background \boldsymbol{p};
  • forward selection driven by a chi-squared mixture LRT \Lambda \stackrel{\text{approx.}}{\sim} \sum_{j=0}^{T} w_j \chi^2_j with weights w_j = \binom{T}{j}/2^T, obtained numerically via qchisq.mixture();
  • the quadratic-form outlier statistic o_k = \tilde{\boldsymbol{q}}_k^{\top}\boldsymbol{G}_a^{-1}\tilde{\boldsymbol{q}}_k / \tilde{v}_k;
  • post-selection MAIN vs G×E classification via Wald zero-equality tests on each QTL’s T-vector of trial-specific effects, giving the final model \boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\tau} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}} \hat{\beta}_j \boldsymbol{x}_j + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}} \hat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}_k^{\top} \boldsymbol{x}_k + \boldsymbol{Z}_u\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{a}_{-s} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{p} + \boldsymbol{e} with main-effect QTL indexed by \mathcal{M} (scalar \hat{\beta}_j) and G×E QTL indexed by \mathcal{I} (trial-specific vector \hat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}_k).

2.1 What’s different in GWAS

The same three GWAS-specific differences noted in the univariate GWAS vignette apply here:

  1. Marker matrix source. qtlAim() uses virtual mid-interval scores from primeCross(type = "interval"). gwasAim() uses the actual panel markers assembled by primePanel(), coded \pm 1 after the x \mapsto x - 1 shift from raw 0/1/2 counts (heterozygotes at 0). Each panel marker is used directly.
  2. Population structure. Diversity panels typically carry both short-range LD and long-range stratification from subpopulations; both are absorbed by the composite additive term via \boldsymbol{G}_a \otimes \boldsymbol{K} in the vm path.
  3. The vm path dominates. Panels almost always satisfy p \gg n, so the multivariate vm formulation \boldsymbol{a} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\, \boldsymbol{G}_a \otimes \boldsymbol{K}) with \boldsymbol{K} = \tfrac{1}{p}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{M}^{\top} is selected automatically.

3 Data Preparation

The pre-analysis pipeline is identical to the univariate GWAS vignette: checkPanel() for a diagnostic scan, filterPanel() for quality filtering with a principled step order, and primePanel() for \pm 1 recoding, chromosome-wise splitting and residual KNN imputation. See the Univariate GWAS vignette for detailed narrative on each function. Here we run all three in a single condensed block:

data(genoGWASraw,  package = "wgAim")
data(mapGWASsim,   package = "wgAim")
data(phenoGWASsim, package = "wgAim")

chk   <- checkPanel(genoGWASraw, mapGWASsim, id = "id")
flt   <- filterPanel(chk)
panel <- primePanel(flt, impute = "knn", knn.k = 5)

cat(sprintf("Prepared panel : %d lines x %d markers across %d chromosomes\n",
            nrow(panel$pheno),
            sum(sapply(panel$geno, function(el) ncol(el$imputed.data))),
            length(panel$geno)))
Prepared panel : 191 lines x 1501 markers across 10 chromosomes

With ~191 lines and ~1450 markers after filtering, the panel sits firmly in the p \gg n regime and gwasAim() will use the vm path automatically at every iteration of forward selection.

3.1 Phenotype setup

The phenotype is a balanced 6-site, 2-replicate MET with Site, id and Rep as factors. We use all 6 sites in the multi-environment analysis (the univariate GWAS vignette used only Env1). The site names are zero-padded to the minimum width needed — for 6 sites this gives Env1..Env6:

pheno <- phenoGWASsim
pheno$id   <- factor(pheno$id)
n.sites    <- nlevels(pheno$Site)
site.width <- nchar(as.character(n.sites))
env.names  <- sprintf(paste0("Env%0", site.width, "d"), seq_len(n.sites))
pheno$Site <- factor(pheno$Site, levels = env.names)
pheno$Rep  <- factor(pheno$Rep)

cat(sprintf("Phenotype : %d rows across %d sites (%d lines x %d reps per site)\n",
            nrow(pheno), nlevels(pheno$Site),
            nlevels(pheno$id), nlevels(pheno$Rep)))
Phenotype : 2400 rows across 6 sites (200 lines x 2 reps per site)

4 Base Model Development

The starting point for a multi-environment gwasAim() analysis is a converged multi-trial base model that captures the experimental design structure and the genetic (co)variance across sites. We build this incrementally, comparing three variance structures for the genetic term.

4.1 Step 1 — Diagonal structure

The simplest multi-site model assumes genetic effects in each site are independent: \boldsymbol{G}_a = \text{diag}(\sigma^2_{g,1}, \ldots, \sigma^2_{g,T}) with no between-site genetic correlations.

base_diag <- asreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ Site + Site:Rep,
  random    = ~ diag(Site):id,
  residual  = ~ dsum(~units | Site),
  data      = pheno,
  na.action = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit     = 100
)
base_diag <- update(base_diag)

4.2 Step 2 — Factor analytic order 1

A single-factor model FA(1) introduces one set of loadings and captures the dominant axis of genotype-by-site interaction:

base_fa1 <- asreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ Site + Site:Rep,
  random    = ~ fa(Site, 1):id,
  residual  = ~ dsum(~units | Site),
  data      = pheno,
  na.action = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit     = 100
)
base_fa1 <- update(base_fa1)

4.3 Step 3 — Factor analytic order 2

A two-factor model FA(2) captures two axes of interaction and provides a richer description of the genetic covariance. This is the model we carry into gwasAim():

base_fa2 <- asreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ Site + Site:Rep,
  random    = ~ fa(Site, 2):id,
  residual  = ~ dsum(~units | Site),
  data      = pheno,
  na.action = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit     = 100
)
base_fa2 <- update(base_fa2)

4.4 Model comparison

We compare the three variance structures using their restricted log-likelihoods and an AIC-style penalty. Parameter counts for n.sites = 6 sites are: diag = 6 (variance per site); fa1 = 6 psi + 6 loadings = 12; fa2 = 6 psi + 12 loadings = 18. Each model also carries the 6 residual variances from dsum(~units | Site):

np <- c(diag = as.integer(   n.sites + n.sites),
        fa1  = as.integer(2L*n.sites + n.sites),
        fa2  = as.integer(3L*n.sites + n.sites))
comp <- data.frame(
  Model      = c("diag(Site):id", "fa(Site, 1):id", "fa(Site, 2):id"),
  Parameters = np,
  LogLik     = round(c(base_diag$loglik, base_fa1$loglik, base_fa2$loglik), 2),
  AIC        = round(c(-2*base_diag$loglik + 2*np["diag"],
                        -2*base_fa1$loglik  + 2*np["fa1"],
                        -2*base_fa2$loglik  + 2*np["fa2"]),   2),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
print(comp, row.names = FALSE)
          Model Parameters LogLik      AIC
  diag(Site):id         12 622.06 -1220.12
 fa(Site, 1):id         18 709.10 -1382.20
 fa(Site, 2):id         24 734.17 -1420.34

FA(2) provides the best balance between fit and parsimony while capturing two axes of genotype-by-site interaction across the six sites.

5 GWAS Mapping — gwasAim()

5.1 Running gwasAim()

The Trait argument activates the multivariate engine, treating "Site" as the grouping factor. Leaving str = NULL (the default) instructs gwasAim() to mirror the variance structure of the base model — here FA(2) — for the composite genome-wide random term, giving consistent modelling of the genetic covariance at every iteration without needing to respecify the order.

We use the default significance level TypeI = 0.05, applied at the family-wise level (the single omnibus multivariate LRT per iteration does not need Bonferroni correction — see the referenced Mathematical Framework section for the argument):

gwas_mv <- gwasAim(
  baseModel        = base_fa2,
  genObj           = panel,
  merge.by         = "id",
  Trait            = "Site",
  str              = NULL,            # mirror the FA(2) structure
  exclusion.window = 20,
  TypeI            = 0.05,
  trace            = FALSE,
  na.action        = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit            = 100
)
cat("Class              :", paste(class(gwas_mv), collapse = ", "), "\n")
Class              : gwasAim, asreml 
cat("Trait              :", gwas_mv$QTL$Trait, "\n")
Trait              : Site 
cat("Markers in panel   :", gwas_mv$QTL$n.markers, "\n")
Markers in panel   : 1501 
cat("Significant markers:", length(gwas_mv$QTL$qtl), "\n")
Significant markers: 5

6 Results

6.1 print() — brief narrative

print() reports the significance threshold, panel size and one line per detected marker with its chromosome, name and cM position, plus a [MAIN] or [INT] tag from the post-selection Wald pruning:

print(gwas_mv, genObj = panel)

GWAS forward selection  TypeI = 0.0500  (1501 markers in panel)

Significant marker on chromosome Chr9: SNP_C09_0068 (60.72 cM) [INTERACTION]

Significant marker on chromosome Chr3: SNP_C03_0128 (110.03 cM) [INTERACTION]

Significant marker on chromosome Chr5: SNP_C05_0094 (90.47 cM) [MAIN]

Significant marker on chromosome Chr2: SNP_C02_0044 (46.00 cM) [MAIN]

Significant marker on chromosome Chr7: SNP_C07_0042 (30.35 cM) [MAIN]

6.2 summary() — final marker table

The multivariate summary() reports one row per site per detected marker. The Trait column identifies the site; MAIN markers appear with a single common Size/Pvalue/Perc.Var/LOD value broadcast to every site; G×E markers show trial-specific effect estimates. Rows are sorted by chromosome, then cM position, then site:

summ_mv <- summary(gwas_mv, genObj = panel)
print(summ_mv)
   Trait Chromosome       Marker dist(cM)    Size   Pvalue Perc.Var   LOD

2   Env1       Chr3 SNP_C03_0128   110.03  0.3295   <1e-06     22.2 18.68
3   Env2       Chr3 SNP_C03_0128   110.03  0.1858   <1e-06     22.2  8.73
4   Env3       Chr3 SNP_C03_0128   110.03  0.1370 0.000124     22.2  3.20
5   Env4       Chr3 SNP_C03_0128   110.03  0.1061 0.001937     22.2  2.09
6   Env5       Chr3 SNP_C03_0128   110.03 -0.0082 0.831729     22.2  0.01
7   Env6       Chr3 SNP_C03_0128   110.03  0.0399  0.26649     22.2  0.27
8   MAIN       Chr5 SNP_C05_0094    90.47 -0.1490   <1e-06     16.9 18.08
9   MAIN       Chr7 SNP_C07_0042    30.35  0.1066   <1e-06      8.6 10.02
10  Env1       Chr9 SNP_C09_0068    60.72 -0.1383  4.3e-05     20.6  3.63
11  Env2       Chr9 SNP_C09_0068    60.72 -0.1801   <1e-06     20.6  9.11
12  Env3       Chr9 SNP_C09_0068    60.72 -0.1930   <1e-06     20.6  7.06
13  Env4       Chr9 SNP_C09_0068    60.72  0.1490    4e-06     20.6  4.57
14  Env5       Chr9 SNP_C09_0068    60.72  0.1455  7.9e-05     20.6  3.38
15  Env6       Chr9 SNP_C09_0068    60.72  0.1741   <1e-06     20.6  5.63

The multi-environment analysis borrows strength across the six sites, so weaker per-site signals combine into detectable joint effects. Compare the recovery here to the single-environment analysis in Env1 from the Univariate GWAS vignette: the MV analysis’s advantage is strongest for QTL with consistent-direction main effects (especially the weakest MAIN, Chr7 +0.125 t/ha), and for G×E QTL like Chr9 whose crossover pattern (±0.180 t/ha) gives large-magnitude signal in every site. Fade patterns like Chr3, whose effect starts at +0.230 t/ha in Env1 and decays to 0 in Env6, give proportionally less joint signal in the later sites and rely on the strong-signal sites for detection.

7 Visualisation — plot()

Six complementary plot types are available via the type argument of plot.gwasAim(). The default for a multivariate object is "manhattan".

7.1 Manhattan plot — type = "manhattan" (default)

A classic Manhattan plot: one point per marker, alternating chromosome backgrounds, significant markers highlighted in sig.col with labels. For a multivariate object the y-axis is the quadratic-form outlier statistic o_k, and one facet is drawn per forward-selection iteration:

plot(gwas_mv, genObj = panel, type = "manhattan", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.2 Genome-wide outlier statistics — type = "outlier"

The outlier plot displays the same multivariate quadratic-form statistic as line traces faceted by iteration. Chromosomal regions that persistently carry signal show up as tall peaks across multiple iterations:

plot(gwas_mv, genObj = panel, type = "outlier", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.3 Scaled genome-wide BLUPs — type = "blups"

For a multivariate GWAS object the BLUPs plot shows one line per site, coloured by site. This display is particularly informative: markers where all site lines move together indicate main-effect signal, while markers where site lines diverge or cross indicate G×E signal (in the raw scaled-BLUP domain, before the model has committed to MAIN vs INT classification):

plot(gwas_mv, genObj = panel, type = "blups", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.4 Allele effects — type = "effects"

The effects lollipop is extended to show one row per site per marker. Main-effect QTL appear as a tight cluster of identically coloured lollipops across all sites; G×E QTL show variation in magnitude or sign across sites:

plot(gwas_mv, genObj = panel, type = "effects")

7.5 Allele contrast — type = "contrast"

The contrast plot shows the total genetic value per line against its allele dosage class (0, 1, 2) at each detected marker, separately for each site. Main-effect markers show the same direction of separation across all site panels; G×E markers show the separation varying or reversing between site panels. As in the univariate vignette, this plot requires data — the augmented phenotype data frame that gwasAim() writes back to the calling environment as yield.data:

plot(gwas_mv, genObj = panel, type = "contrast",
     data = yield.data, ncol = 3)

7.6 Iteration heatmap — type = "heatmap"

The heatmap gives a compact genome × iteration view, filling each cell with the multivariate outlier statistic. This makes it easy to see which chromosomal regions carried persistent multi-environment signal across iterations:

plot(gwas_mv, genObj = panel, type = "heatmap", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.7 Linkage map overlay — linkMap()

linkMap() overlays the detected markers on the panel map:

linkMap(gwas_mv, genObj = panel, marker.names = "markers")

8 Iteration Diagnostics — aimTrace()

8.1 LRT trace — plot = "lrt"

The mixture chi-squared threshold (shown as a dashed line) reflects the T-dimensional nature of the test — it lies above the univariate \chi^2_1 threshold because the test jointly evaluates effects across all T = 6 sites:

aimTrace(gwas_mv, plot = "lrt", print.out = FALSE)

8.2 Effect stability — plot = "stability"

The stability plot traces the per-site allele effect ± 1 SE for each detected marker across iterations. Stable main-effect markers show all site lines tracking closely together; G×E markers show site lines that are separated or diverge as further markers enter the model. The panel is laid out with sites as rows and markers as columns, with a [MAIN] or [INT] tag in each column header:

aimTrace(gwas_mv, plot = "stability", print.out = FALSE)

9 Summary

The complete multi-environment GWAS pipeline illustrated in this vignette is:

# 1. Pre-analysis: check -> filter -> prime the diversity panel
chk   <- checkPanel(genoGWASraw, mapGWASsim, id = "id")
flt   <- filterPanel(chk)
panel <- primePanel(flt, impute = "knn", knn.k = 5)

# 2. Phenotype setup
pheno       <- phenoGWASsim
pheno$id    <- factor(pheno$id)
pheno$Site  <- factor(pheno$Site)   # ensures Env1..Env6 ordering
pheno$Rep   <- factor(pheno$Rep)

# 3. Multi-trial base model progression (diag -> FA1 -> FA2)
base_diag <- asreml(yield ~ Site + Site:Rep,
                    random   = ~ diag(Site):id,
                    residual = ~ dsum(~units | Site),
                    data = pheno, na.action = na.method(x = "include"))
base_fa1  <- asreml(yield ~ Site + Site:Rep,
                    random   = ~ fa(Site, 1):id,
                    residual = ~ dsum(~units | Site),
                    data = pheno, na.action = na.method(x = "include"))
base_fa2  <- asreml(yield ~ Site + Site:Rep,
                    random   = ~ fa(Site, 2):id,
                    residual = ~ dsum(~units | Site),
                    data = pheno, na.action = na.method(x = "include"))

# 4. Multi-environment GWAS forward selection (str = NULL mirrors FA(2))
gwas_mv <- gwasAim(base_fa2, genObj = panel, merge.by = "id",
                   Trait = "Site", str = NULL,
                   TypeI = 0.05, exclusion.window = 20,
                   na.action = na.method(x = "include"), maxit = 100)

# 5. Results
summary(gwas_mv, genObj = panel)                 # MAIN/INT table by site
plot(gwas_mv,    genObj = panel)                 # Manhattan (default)
plot(gwas_mv,    genObj = panel, type = "outlier")
plot(gwas_mv,    genObj = panel, type = "blups")
plot(gwas_mv,    genObj = panel, type = "effects")
plot(gwas_mv,    genObj = panel, type = "contrast",
                 data = yield.data, ncol = 3)
plot(gwas_mv,    genObj = panel, type = "heatmap")
aimTrace(gwas_mv, plot = "lrt",       print.out = FALSE)
aimTrace(gwas_mv, plot = "stability", print.out = FALSE)
linkMap(gwas_mv,  genObj = panel)
